issues.legal_issue: Compensation for damage caused by overhead electrical lines must be determined on the circumstances of each property rather than by a fixed formula or rate of return.
material_facts: Trees were cut and removed to draw an overhead high-voltage electrical line across private property.
The compensation assessments had used differing approaches, including annuity calculations based on different rates of return and different percentages of diminution in land value.

The relevant circumstances could include the land’s location and value, the line’s distance above and extent across the land, whether it passed over a small strip or through the middle of the property, and any loss of the owner’s ability to use the land for its intended purpose.
issues.conclusion: The amount of compensation could not be determined by a fixed formula or rate applicable to every case. The assessments had to be reconsidered on the merits of each case, having regard to its particular facts.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 10(d) and 16(3) of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885, compensation for damage from exercising the power to place a line is determined by the District Judge if disputed. Section 51 of the Indian Electricity Act, 1910 permits the relevant powers of the telegraph authority to be conferred for placing electrical lines. The Court held that the statutory purpose and the circumstances of the individual case guide compensation; the approaches in Kerala Electricity Board v. Thomas, K.S.E. Board v. Marthoma Rubber Co. Ltd., and Kumba Amma v. K.S.E.B. may assist but do not establish a universal formula. The Court also referred to Land Acquisition Officer v. Kamandana Ramakrishna Rao, Kapur Singh Mistry v. Financial Commission, State of Haryana v. Gurcharan Singh, and Airports Authority of India v. Satyagopal Roy in recognizing yield as a relevant compensation method.

rule.if: compensation_appeal_for_overhead_line and private_property_is_crossed_by_line and (property_value_or_use_is_affected or trees_are_removed)

predicates.compensation_appeal_for_overhead_line: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for an overhead electrical line.
predicates.private_property_is_crossed_by_line: An overhead line is placed across or over property belonging to a private owner.
predicates.property_value_or_use_is_affected: The line’s placement diminishes the property’s value or impairs its intended use.
predicates.trees_are_removed: Trees on the property are cut or removed for the line.

issues.definition: When an overhead line crosses private property and affects its value or use or requires tree removal, compensation must be assessed on the circumstances of that property rather than by a universal formula.

issues.legal_issue: The yield of destroyed fruit-bearing trees is a relevant consideration in determining compensation for their destruction.
material_facts: Trees were cut and removed in connection with the drawing of an overhead electrical line.
The Court considered how compensation for fruit-bearing trees should be assessed and referred to decisions recognizing compensation based on tree yield as relevant.
issues.conclusion: Compensation for fruit-bearing trees depends on the facts and circumstances of each case, and yield may be relevant to its assessment.
issues.legal_principle: Applying the case-specific approach to compensation under Sections 10(d) and 16(3) of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885, the Court treated yield as a relevant basis for assessing compensation. It relied on Land Acquisition Officer v. Kamandana Ramakrishna Rao, Kapur Singh Mistry v. Financial Commission, State of Haryana v. Gurcharan Singh, and Airports Authority of India v. Satyagopal Roy, which recognized yield-based assessment in determining compensation for trees.

predicates.compensation_appeal_for_tree_removal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for trees removed for an overhead line.
predicates.fruit_bearing_trees_are_removed: Fruit-bearing trees are cut or removed from property.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns compensation for removed fruit-bearing trees, their yield is a relevant consideration in assessing compensation.

issues.legal_issue: A compensation determination that changes land value or diminution without reasons or analysis of the supporting material cannot be sustained.
material_facts: A lower court had fixed a land value and a percentage of diminution in value.
A High Court judgment increased both figures without giving reasons or analyzing the material on record.
The appeals concerned compensation assessments that the Supreme Court directed the High Court to reconsider on the merits of each case.
issues.conclusion: The impugned determinations could not be sustained; they were set aside and the matters were remitted for fresh consideration on their individual merits.
issues.legal_principle: Compensation must be determined with regard to the purpose of the governing law and the facts and material in the particular case. A change to compensation figures requires an assessment grounded in the relevant circumstances and record, rather than an unexplained alteration. The Court applied Sections 10(d) and 16(3) of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885, and its case-specific approach to compensation.

predicates.compensation_appeal_involves_changed_ass: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a changed determination of compensation.
predicates.changed_assessment_lacks_reasons_or_mate: The court that changed the assessment gave no reasons or failed to analyze the supporting material.

issues.definition: When an appellate compensation assessment is changed without reasons or analysis of the material, that unsupported determination cannot stand.
